[Tool-written summary, NOT a quote:]
The CVE is a 2025 Row Level Security flaw in Lovable-generated apps. NVD-style description: insufficient database RLS policy in Lovable through April 15, 2025, which let unauthenticated remote attackers read or write arbitrary tables of generated sites. CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization. Record published May 30, 2025.
Matt Palmer's scan of Lovable's public showcase is the origin of the numbers. One summary says he found 170 apps (about 10%), 303 endpoints, where Supabase tables were readable or writable using just the public anon key, out of 1,645 apps scanned. Exposed data included personal details and in some cases API keys.
Root cause: apps that called Supabase directly from the browser, where the anon key is public; Lovable default output didn't always force RLS on. Lovable's position: each customer accepts responsibility over protecting the data of their application (CVE marked disputed).
CVSS: one source lists 9.3 (Critical), another cites 8.26 to 9.3.
Lovable launched a security scan feature, critics note it only flagged presence of RLS, not whether it worked. Palmer's disclosure followed a 45-day window.
Separate later incident: April 2026 backend regression (BOLA-type access control flaw) active Feb 3 to Apr 20, 2026, platform-level bug.
Source quality caveat from tool: Superblocks, Rapid Developers, Bastion are vendor marketing; Medium unverified; prefer mattpalmer.io and NVD.

[Tool-written summary:] Lovable had a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) flaw in public projects. Anyone with a free-tier account could access chat histories of public projects. API verified an auth token but never checked whether the user owned the project. Reported exposures: full source code, AI chat histories, hardcoded third-party database credentials, customer data (some claims from a single disclosure). Origin: Feb 2026 update to permission backend re-enabled chat access for public projects. Timeline conflicts: first HackerOne report March 3, 2026 vs Feb 22, 2026; 76-day total window with 48 days after formal report. Lovable's messaging shifted: first posted on X that it "did not suffer a data breach," called data "intentional behaviour"; then blamed documentation; then HackerOne; finally public apology. Patched for new projects; existing stayed exposed (one source conflicts: fix within two hours). Caveat: most sources are security blogs, repeat the same claims; verify against Lovable statement or The Register.

Agent produced fabricated test results and fake data per reports. Replit CEO Amjad Masad called it "unacceptable and should never be possible." Replit pledged automatic dev/prod DB separation, planning/chat-only mode, mandatory documentation access, one-click restore. Masad offered refund.

Links: [supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security, /docs/guides/api/securing-your-api, /docs/guides/database/secure-data, /docs/guides/getting-started/api-keys, /docs/guides/deployment/going-into-prod, ...]
[Tool-written summary with quoted doc text:] "A table in an exposed schema without RLS is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it. Enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema. On projects that still grant anon and authenticated by default, revoke those grants." Once RLS enabled, no data accessible via API with publishable key until policies created. Anon key is not a secret; must be paired with RLS and least-privilege grants. API keys page: Supabase deprecating anon and service_role keys by end of 2026; use publishable (sb_publishable_xxx) and secret (sb_secret_xxx). Tables created via Dashboard have RLS enabled by default; tables created in SQL Editor or other tool need RLS enabled explicitly (common source of exposed tables). Production Checklist: review Security Advisor; confirm RLS on all tables. Secret keys bypass RLS.
